source_refs.note: Topic printed as 2.11.2, printed page 42: n-type formation (Figure 2.18).

blocks.text: When impurity atoms with five valence electrons, such as phosphorus, are added to the pure semiconductor, some silicon atoms are replaced by the pentavalent phosphorus atoms. The silicon atoms around them can make four bonds, and the fifth electron of the impurity is an extra electron. These impurity atoms contribute extra electrons to the crystal lattice, which are free to move and act as negative charge carriers. The result is an N-type semiconductor that conducts electricity when connected to an external source.

blocks.alt: Two panels of a silicon lattice. Left: an aluminium atom, with three valence electrons, sits among four silicon atoms; one of its four bonds is missing an electron, leaving a hole, so it is a p-type semiconductor. Right: a phosphorus atom, with five valence electrons, forms four bonds and has one free electron left over, so it is an n-type semiconductor.
blocks.caption: Doping and the formation of p-type and n-type semiconductors (original diagram after Figure 2.18).
